The technical documentation kept on the authority's premises (Annex IV) must contain a post-market monitoring plan. Under Article 72(3), the post-market monitoring plan is part of the technical documentation referred to in Annex IV. This plan underpins the post-market monitoring system, which under Article 72(2) must actively and systematically collect, document and analyse relevant data on the performance of high-risk AI systems throughout their lifetime, allowing the provider to evaluate the system's continuous compliance with the requirements set out in Chapter III, Section 2.

(Note: under Article 72(2), the post-market monitoring obligation does not cover sensitive operational data of deployers that are law-enforcement authorities.)

Biometrics. Annex VIII, point 12 states that the electronic instructions for use "shall not be provided for high-risk AI systems in the areas of law enforcement or migration, asylum and border control management referred to in Annex III, points 1, 6 and 7." Since points 6 and 7 correspond to law enforcement and migration/asylum/border control, the additional exempt area is point 1, which concerns biometrics (as identified in Recital 159).

Under Article 36(2), the procedures in Articles 29 and 30 apply to extensions of the scope of a notification. Accordingly, per Article 29(2), the application for notification must be accompanied by:

- a description of the conformity assessment activities, the conformity assessment module(s), and the types of AI systems for which the body claims competence;
- an accreditation certificate, where one exists, issued by a national accreditation body attesting that the body fulfils the requirements laid down in Article 31; and
- any valid document related to existing designations of the applicant notified body under any other Union harmonisation legislation.

Where the body cannot provide an accreditation certificate, it must instead provide the notifying authority with all documentary evidence necessary for the verification, recognition and regular monitoring of its compliance with Article 31 (Article 29(3)).

Under Article 74(1)(a), for the purposes of applying Regulation (EU) 2019/1020 to AI systems, any reference to an economic operator is to be understood as including all operators identified in Article 2(1) of this Regulation.

Under Article 91, the Commission could have requested the documentation drawn up by the provider in accordance with Articles 53 and 55, or any additional information necessary for assessing the provider's compliance with the Regulation.

This documentation includes, per Article 53(1), the technical documentation of the model (its training and testing process and evaluation results, at minimum the elements in Annex XI) and the information and documentation made available to downstream providers integrating the model (at minimum the elements in Annex XII).

By putting its trademark on the system, the distributor is considered a provider under Article 25(1)(a) and becomes subject to the provider obligations under Article 16. Among those, Article 16(c) requires it to have a quality management system in place which complies with Article 17.

Because the digital CE marking was affixed in a way that does not comply with Article 48(2) (which requires that it be easily accessible via the interface from which the system is accessed), this is a violation of Article 48 and thus constitutes formal non-compliance under Article 83(1)(a). The market surveillance authority must require the relevant provider to put an end to the non-compliance within a period it may prescribe. Where the non-compliance persists, the authority must take appropriate and proportionate measures to restrict or prohibit the high-risk AI system being made available on the market, or to ensure it is recalled or withdrawn from the market without delay.

The EU AI Act applies from 2 August 2026. However, there are exceptions: Chapters I and II apply from 2 February 2025; Chapter III Section 4, Chapter V, Chapter VII, Chapter XII and Article 78 apply from 2 August 2025 (except Article 101); and Article 6(1) and its corresponding obligations apply from 2 August 2027.

Informed consent must be dated and documented, and a copy must be given to the subjects of testing or their legal representative.

High-impact capabilities in general-purpose AI models means capabilities that match or exceed the capabilities recorded in the most advanced general-purpose AI models.

A general-purpose AI model is presumed to have high-impact capabilities when the cumulative amount of computation used for its training, measured in floating point operations, is greater than 10²⁵.

Where an AI system is based on a general-purpose AI model and both the model and the system are developed/provided by the same provider, the AI Office supervises it at Union level, with the powers of a market surveillance authority. In all other cases, national market surveillance authorities are responsible.

Importers must indicate their name, registered trade name or registered trade mark, and the address at which they can be contacted—on the high-risk AI system and on its packaging or accompanying documentation, where applicable.

Before putting into service a high-risk AI system listed in Annex III (with the exception of point 2), a deploying public authority must:

- Register themselves, select the system, and register its use in the EU database referred to in Article 71 (Article 49(3)).
- As a body governed by public law, perform a fundamental rights impact assessment covering the elements listed in Article 27(1), and once performed, notify the market surveillance authority of its results, submitting the filled-out template (Article 27(3)).

For high-risk AI systems referred to in points 1, 6 and 7 of Annex III in the areas of law enforcement, migration, asylum and border control management, the registration must be made in a secure non-public section of the EU database (Article 49(4)).

Providers must grant market surveillance authorities:

- **Full access** to the documentation as well as the training, validation and testing data sets used for the development of high-risk AI systems—where relevant and limited to what is necessary, and where appropriate through application programming interfaces (APIs) or other technical means enabling remote access, subject to security safeguards (Art. 74(12)).

- **Access to the source code** of the high-risk AI system, but only upon a reasoned request and only when both conditions are met: (a) access is necessary to assess conformity with the requirements in Chapter III, Section 2; and (b) testing/auditing procedures and verifications based on the provided data and documentation have been exhausted or proved insufficient (Art. 74(13)).

Any information or documentation obtained must be treated in accordance with the confidentiality obligations in Article 78 (Art. 74(14)).
In the case of SMEs, including start-ups, each fine shall be up to the percentages or amount referred to in paragraphs 3, 4 and 5 of Article 99, whichever thereof is lower.
Privacy and cybersecurity risk management considerations and approaches are applicable in the design, development, deployment, evaluation, and use of AI systems.

Per MANAGE 3.1, AI risks and benefits from third-party resources must be regularly monitored, and risk controls must be applied and documented.

Suggested actions to achieve this include:
- Applying organizational risk tolerance and documenting risk management plans/practices to third-party AI technology, personnel, or resources.
- Identifying and maintaining documentation for third-party AI systems and components.
- Establishing testing, evaluation, validation and verification processes without exposing proprietary algorithms.
- Establishing processes to identify beneficial use and risk indicators (e.g., inconsistent release schedules, sparse documentation, incomplete change management).
- Enabling third parties to report known/potential vulnerabilities, risks, or biases.
- Verifying contingency processes for mission-critical third-party systems.
- Monitoring third-party systems for negative impacts and trustworthiness risks.
- Decommissioning third-party systems that exceed risk tolerances.

Additionally, per GOVERN 6.1, policies and procedures must be in place that address AI risks associated with third-party entities, including risks of infringing a third party's intellectual property or other rights. Per MAP 4.2, internal risk controls for third-party AI technologies must be identified and documented.

Transparency answers the question of "what happened" in the system. Explainability answers the question of "how" a decision was made in the system. Interpretability answers the question of "why" a decision was made by the system and its meaning or context to the user.
Organizational practices must be in place to enable AI testing, identification of incidents, and information sharing (GOVERN 4.3).
The physical synthesis, development, production, and use of chemical or biological agents will still require both applicable expertise and supporting materials and infrastructure.

The parent subcategory (MEASURE 2.2) requires that evaluations involving human subjects meet applicable requirements (including human subject protection) and are representative of the relevant population.

The About context adds that:
- Protection of human subjects is required by law for federally funded research and is a domain-specific requirement for some disciplines.
- Standard human subjects protection procedures include protecting the welfare and interests of human subjects, designing evaluations to minimize risks to subjects, and completing mandatory training regarding legal requirements and expectations.
- Evaluations utilizing human subjects or their data should reflect the population within the context of use, since non-representative data may lead to inaccurate assessments or harmful outcomes.
- Organizations can connect human subjects data collection and dataset practices to AI system contexts and purposes, in close collaboration with AI Actors from relevant domains.
